question: Which statement best describes The <form> element: action & method?
options: Only controls with a name attribute are submitted, and the name becomes the key in the resulting key=value pairs. A control without a name is ignored entirely. So the data the server receives is a map of each control's name to its current value (or its checked value, for checkboxes/radios).

A <form> wraps controls and defines submission. The action attribute is the URL the data goes to; the method attribute is the HTTP verb used to send it (GET or POST). With no action, the form submits to the current page's URL. The browser builds the request from the form's controls when a submit button is activated.

<fieldset> groups related controls (e.g., a shipping address) and renders a border by default; <legend> gives the group an accessible caption announced by screen readers. Grouping is especially important for radio button sets, where the legend describes the question the radios answer.

GET appends form data to the URL as a query string (?q=hello&page=2) — it's idempotent, bookmarkable, and suited to searches and filters, but visible and length-limited. POST puts data in the request body — used for changes (creating accounts, posting), for larger payloads, and for sensitive data that shouldn't sit in the URL or browser history.

enctype controls how POST data is encoded. The default application/x-www-form-urlencoded sends key=value pairs. multipart/form-data is required for file uploads (<input type=file>) because it can carry binary data and filenames. text/plain exists but is rarely used. GET requests always use URL encoding regardless of enctype.

question: Which statement best describes The name attribute & form data?
options: By default, submitting a form triggers a full-page navigation/reload. In single-page apps you intercept the submit event and call event.preventDefault(), then read values (often via the FormData API) and send them yourself with fetch. This keeps the user on the page while still respecting native validation and Enter-to-submit.

options: <fieldset> groups related controls (e.g., a shipping address) and renders a border by default; <legend> gives the group an accessible caption announced by screen readers. Grouping is especially important for radio button sets, where the legend describes the question the radios answer.

On submit the browser runs native validation, serializes named controls per the method/enctype, builds an HTTP request to the action URL, and sends it. The server parses the body or query string, processes it, and responds (a redirect, a new page, or JSON for fetch). Understanding this round-trip explains why name, method, and enctype matter.
